source_text: Προφανεῖς μὲν οὖν καὶ πᾶσαι αἱ ἄλλαι ἀρεταί, αἱ παρὰ τῷ Μωυσεῖ ἀναγεγραμμέναι, ἀρχὴν Ἕλλησι παντὸς τοῦ ἠθικοῦ τόπου παρασχόμεναι, ἀνδρείαν λέγω καὶ σωφροσύνην καὶ φρόνησιν καὶ δικαιοσύνην καρτερίαν τε καὶ ὑπομονὴν καὶ τὴν σεμνότητα καὶ ἐγκράτειαν τήν τε ἐπὶ τούτοις εὐσέβειαν. ἀλλ’ ἡ μὲν εὐσέβεια παντί που δήλη τὸ ἀνωτάτω καὶ πρεσβύτατον αἴτιον σέβειν καὶ τιμᾶν καὶ διδάσκουσα. καὶ δικαιοσύνην δὲ αὐτὸς ὁ νόμος παρίστησι παιδεύων τήν τε φρόνησιν διὰ τῆς τῶν αἰσθητῶν εἰδώλων ἀποχῆς καὶ τῆς πρὸς τὸν ποιητὴν καὶ πατέρα τῶν ὅλων προσκληρώσεως, ἀφ’ ἧς δόξης οἷον πηγῆς πᾶσα σύνεσις αὔξεται. θυσίαι γὰρ ἀνόμων βδέλυγμα κυρίῳ, εὐχαὶ δὲ κατευθυνόντων δεκταὶ παρ’ αὐτῷ. ἐπεὶ οιαῦτα καὶ τὰ παρὰ Ἡσαΐᾳ· τί μοι πλῆθος τῶν θυσιῶν ὑμῶν ὑμῶν; λέγει κύριος, καὶ πᾶσα ἡ περικοπή· λῦε πάντα σύνδεσμον ἀδικίας· αὕτη γὰρ θυσία θεῷ δεκτή, καρδία συντετριμμένη καὶ ζητοῦσα τὸν πεπλακότα. ζυγὰ δόλια βδέλυγμα ἔναντι θεοῦ, στάθμιον δὲ δίκαιον δεκτὸν αὐτῷ. ἐντεῦθεν ζυγὸν μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν Πυθαγόρας παραινεῖ. δικαιοσύνη δὲ δολία εἴρηται ἡ τῶν αἱρέσεων ἐπαγγελία, καὶ γλῶσσα μὲν ἀδίκων ἐξολεῖται, στόμα δὲ δικαίων ἀποστάζει σοφίαν. ἀλλὰ γὰρ τοὺς σοφοὺς καὶ φρονίμους φαύλους καλοῦσιν. μακρὸν δ’ ἂν εἴη περὶ τῶν ἀρετῶν τούτων μαρτυρίας παρατίθεσθαι, ἁπάσης ταύτας ἐξυμνούσης τῆς γραφῆς. ἐπεὶ δ’ οὖν τὴν μὲν ἀνδρείαν ὁρίζονται ἐπιστήμην δεινῶν καὶ οὐ δεινῶν καὶ τῶν μεταξύ, τὴν δὲ σωφροσύνην ἕξιν ἐν αἱρέσει καὶ φυγῇ σῴζουσαν τὰ τῆς φρονήσεως κρίματα, παράκειται τε τῇ μὲν ἀνδρείᾳ ἥ τε ὑπομονή, ἣν καρτερίαν καλοῦσιν, ἐπιστήμην ἐμμενετέων καὶ οὐκ ἐμμενετέων, ἥ τε μεγαλοψυχία, ἐπιστήμη τῶν συμβαινόντων ὑπεραίρουσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῇ σωφροσύνῃ ἡ εὐλάβεια, ἔκκλισις οὖσα σὺν λόγῳ. Φυλακὴ δὲ τῶν ἐντολῶν, τήρησις οὖσα αὐτῶν ἀβλαβής, περιποίησίς ἐστιν ἀσφαλείας βίου. καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ἄνευ ἀνδρείας καρτερικὸν εἶναι οὐδὲ μὴν ἄνευ σωφροσύνης ἐγκρατῆ. ἀντακολουθοῦσι δὲ ἀλλήλαις αἱ ἀρεταί, καἰ παρ’ ᾧ αἱ τῶν ἀρετῶν ἀκολουθίαι, παρὰ τούτῳ καὶ ἡ σωτηρία, τήρησις οὖσα τοῦ εὖ ἔχοντος. εἰκότως ἔτι περὶ τούτων διαλαβόντες τῶν ἀρετῶν περὶ πασῶν ἂν εἴημεν ἐσκεμμένοι, ὅτι ὁ μίαν ἔχων ἀρετὴν γνωστικῶς πάσας ἔχει διὰ τὴν ἀντακολουθίαν. αὐτίκα ἡ ἐγκράτεια διάθεσίς ἐστιν ἀνυπέρβατος τῶν κατὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον φανέντων. ἐγκρατεύεται δὲ ὁ κατέχων τὰς παρὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον ὁρμὰς ἢ ὁ κατέχων αὑτὸν ὥστε μὴ ὁρμᾶν παρὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον.
thought_title: Virtues in Greek and Christian Thought
pass_a_gloss: The other virtues, which are written by Moses, are evident and they provide a starting point for all ethical matters for the Greeks, I mean courage and self-control and prudence and justice and patience and perseverance and dignity and self-control and the piety that is based on these. But piety is evident to everyone as the highest and most ancient cause to reverence and honor and it teaches. And the law itself presents justice, teaching prudence through the avoidance of sensory idols and the calling towards the creator and father of all, from which glory, as if from a source, all understanding increases. For sacrifices of the lawless are an abomination to the Lord, but the prayers of those who are guided are acceptable to him. Since also the things from Isaiah say: what is the multitude of your sacrifices to me, says the Lord, and the whole passage says: loose every bond of injustice, for this is a sacrifice acceptable to God, a heart that is broken and seeking the one who has been afflicted. False scales are an abomination before God, but a just balance is acceptable to him. From this, Pythagoras advises not to exceed the balance. But the justice of the sects is said to be false, and the tongue of the unrighteous will be destroyed, but the mouth of the righteous will overflow with wisdom. But they call the wise and prudent ones worthless. It would be long to present testimonies about these virtues, which all of scripture praises. Since, therefore, they define courage as the knowledge of what is fearful and not fearful and what is in between, and self-control as a state that saves the judgments of prudence in choice and avoidance, perseverance, which they call patience, is placed beside courage, which is the knowledge of what endures and what does not endure, and magnanimity, which is the knowledge of what happens, exceeding, but also caution is placed beside self-control, which is a turning away with reason. The guarding of the commandments, being the blameless keeping of them, is the acquisition of the safety of life. And it is not possible to be patient without courage or self-controlled without self-control. The virtues follow one another, and where the followings of the virtues are, there also is salvation, which is the keeping of what is good. It is likely that, having taken up these virtues, we would be concerned with all of them, because the one who has one virtue knowingly has all of them through their following one another. Immediately, self-control is a disposition that is invincible regarding the things that appear according to the right reason. And one is self-controlled who holds back the impulses that are contrary to the right reason or who holds himself back so as not to be impelled contrary to the right reason.

choices.why: The verb ἐγκρατεύεται is in the passive voice, indicating that the subject is being controlled or restrained.
The phrase ὀρθὸν λόγον refers to the correct or proper reasoning.
The verb ἀντακολουθοῦσι is in the present tense, indicating a continuous or ongoing action.

bible_refs.note: The passage from Isaiah is quoted in the text.

pass_b_english: Clearly, all the other virtues recorded in Moses—courage, self-control, prudence, justice, patience, perseverance, dignity, self-control, and the piety that rests on these—provide the Greeks with a starting point for every ethical matter. Piety, however, is evident to everyone as the highest and most ancient cause to reverence and honor, and it teaches this. The law itself also presents justice, instructing prudence through the avoidance of sensory idols and the calling toward the Creator and Father of all; from that glory, as from a source, all understanding grows. For the sacrifices of the lawless are an abomination to the Lord, but the prayers of those who are guided are acceptable to him (Isaiah 1:11-17). The passage in Isaiah likewise says: "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord," and the whole text continues: "Loose every bond of injustice, for this is a sacrifice acceptable to God, a heart that is broken and seeking the one who has been afflicted." False scales are an abomination before God, but a just balance is acceptable to him; from this Pythagoras advises not to exceed the balance. Yet the justice of the sects is called false, and the tongue of the unrighteous will be destroyed, but the mouth of the righteous will overflow with wisdom. Still, they call the wise and prudent worthless. It would take too long to set out testimonies about these virtues, since all Scripture sings their praise. Since they define courage as the knowledge of what is fearful, what is not fearful, and what lies between, and self-control as a state that preserves the judgments of prudence in choice and avoidance, perseverance—which they call patience—stands alongside courage as the knowledge of what endures and what does not, and magnanimity stands there as the knowledge that rises above what happens; likewise caution stands alongside self-control as a turning away guided by reason. The keeping of the commandments, which is their blameless observance, is the securing of safety in life. One cannot be patient without courage, nor self-controlled without self-control. The virtues follow one another, and where the sequence of the virtues is found, there also is salvation, which is the preservation of what is good. It is reasonable, then, that by taking up these virtues we would be versed in all of them, because the one who possesses one virtue knowingly possesses them all through their mutual sequence. Self-control, in short, is an invincible disposition toward the things that appear according to right reason. A person is self-controlled who restrains the impulses that run contrary to right reason, or who restrains himself so as not to be driven contrary to right reason.
